from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    text=p.extract_text()
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
    texts.append(f'\\n\\n=== PAGE {i} ===\\n\\n'+text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The paper proposes a useful, well-motivated combination of density-ratio-based Bayesian optimization and graph-based semi-supervised learning. Exploiting the geometry of unevaluated candidates is particularly natural for optimization over finite pools, and the relationship to BORE, LFBO, and classical label propagation is explained clearly.

The experiments cover continuous synthetic functions, finite-pool optimization, tabular hyperparameter optimization, neural architecture search, and an image-derived search problem. Comparisons against multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers and GP acquisitions, with 20 repetitions and standard errors, provide meaningful evidence of competitive performance. Figures 2, 3, and 6 show substantial gains in several settings.

The appendices include useful sensitivity studies covering kernel bandwidth, unlabeled sample size, sampling distribution, pool subsampling, and classification thresholds. The paper also acknowledges computational limitations and that existing semi-supervised learning guarantees do not directly apply to sequential optimization.
weaknesses: The principal benefit attributed to unlabeled data is insufficiently isolated. Figure 12 includes a valuable no-transduction/Nadaraya–Watson control, but fixes the kernel parameter at beta=0.5, whereas the headline experiments learn beta and Figure 11 demonstrates substantial sensitivity to it. The control also produces mixed results, sometimes outperforming semi-supervision. A supervised kernel classifier with comparable bandwidth selection, together with an ablation of the random tie-breaking heuristic, is needed to distinguish the effects of unlabeled data from kernel choice and acquisition optimization. This uncertainty about the central contribution drives my weak-reject recommendation.

The proposed explanation for improved exploration remains inadequately supported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observed inputs does not establish Assumption 4.1: nearby observations with opposite threshold labels can still be connected through high-density regions. Appendix C does not demonstrate that adding unlabeled points reduces the stated margin or expands useful positive-class regions. Its cited theory is explicitly inapplicable to adaptively collected BO data. The exploration claim therefore needs direct supporting measurements or narrower wording; larger positive-class regions alone do not establish a better exploration–exploitation balance.

Important implementation details remain unspecified, including input scaling, numerical settings for label propagation/spreading, initialization and bounds for bandwidth optimization, and how acquisition maximization handles finite pools and discrete variables. These choices materially affect distance-based predictions and reproducibility. Baseline fitting and optimization details are also incomplete. Separately, there is a fixable mathematical inconsistency: the column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P=WD^{-1}, whereas the text states P=D^{-1}W and subsequently uses P transpose.

The evidence for generality beyond small continuous domains is limited. All continuous synthetic benchmarks are two-dimensional. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses a representation pretrained on 440,000 examples with labels directly identifying the number being minimized. Although the representation is shared across methods and uses separate training data, it provides unusually favorable task-related geometry and is limited evidence for generic high-dimensional black-box optimization.

Practical computational competitiveness is not established. Figure 14 measures pool-size scaling within the proposed methods using fixed beta, while the main experiments repeatedly optimize beta and use 1,000 acquisition-optimization starts. End-to-end timing against the baselines would clarify whether the evaluation savings justify the additional graph construction and optimization costs.
